tools.name: WolframLanguageContext
tools.title: Wolfram Language Context
tools.description: Uses semantic search to retrieve information from various sources that can be used to help write Wolfram Language code. Always use this tool at the start of new conversations or if the topic changes to ensure you have up-to-date relevant information. This uses semantic search, so the context argument should be written in natural language (not a search query) and contain as much detail as possible.

context.description: A detailed summary of what the user is trying to achieve or learn about.

tools.name: WolframLanguageEvaluator
tools.title: Wolfram Language Evaluator
tools.description:
Evaluates Wolfram Language code for the user in a Wolfram Language kernel.
Do not ask permission to evaluate code.
You have read access to local files.
Always use the Wolfram context tool before using this tool to make sure you have the most up-to-date information.

Use `\[FreeformPrompt]["query"]` to parse natural language into Wolfram Language expressions (like ctrl+= in notebooks). Always use this for `Quantity`, `Entity`, `EntityClass`, etc. It composes freely: `ColorNegate[\[FreeformPrompt]["picture of a cat"]]`.

Examples:
```
\[FreeformPrompt]["France population"]  (* Entity property value *)
\[FreeformPrompt]["123 terawatt hours"] (* Quantity *)
```

The argument MUST be a string literal — it parses before evaluation, so runtime construction will not work.

code.description: The Wolfram Language code to evaluate.

timeConstraint.description: The time constraint for the evaluation. Uses the server's configured default if not specified.

session.description: An opaque session ID returned by a previous call to this tool. Pass it to continue that conversation's isolated session (its definitions, line numbers, and history). Omit it to start a new session; the response returns a new ID that you should reuse on subsequent calls in this conversation.

tools.name: ReadNotebook
tools.title: Read Notebook
tools.description: Reads the contents of a Wolfram notebook (.nb) as markdown text.

notebook.description: The Wolfram notebook to read, specified as a file path or a NotebookObject[...]

tools.name: WriteNotebook
tools.title: Write Notebook
tools.description: Converts markdown text to a Wolfram notebook and saves it to a file.

file.description: The file to write the notebook to (must end in .nb). Any missing parent directories are created automatically.

overwrite.description: Whether to overwrite an existing file (default is False).

markdown.description: The markdown text to write to a notebook.

tools.name: SymbolDefinition
tools.title: Symbol Definition
tools.description:
Retrieves the definitions of one or more Wolfram Language symbols and returns them in a readable markdown format.
The tool generates clean, formatted definition strings by intelligently managing the context path to minimize fully qualified symbol names.

Use fully qualified symbol names (e.g., System`Plus, Wolfram`AgentTools`CreateMCPServer) if the context is known.
Multiple symbols can be requested by separating them with commas.

symbols.description: The symbol name (or multiple names, comma separated).

includeContextDetails.description: Whether to include a JSON map showing which symbols belong to which contexts (default: false).

maxLength.description: Maximum character length for output before truncation (default: 10000).

tools.name: CodeInspector
tools.title: Code Inspector
tools.description: Inspects Wolfram Language code using the CodeInspector package and returns a formatted report of issues found. The tool supports inspecting code strings, individual files, or entire directories of Wolfram Language source files.

code.description: Wolfram Language code string to inspect.

file.description: File or directory path to inspect. For directories, recursively inspects all .wl, .m, and .wls files.

tagExclusions.description: Comma-separated list of tags to exclude (e.g., "UnusedVariable,SuspiciousSessionSymbol").

severityExclusions.description: Comma-separated list of severities to exclude. Default: "Formatting,Scoping". Available: Fatal, Error, Warning, Scoping, Remark, Formatting.

confidenceLevel.description: Minimum confidence level (0.0 to 1.0). Default: 0.75. Issues below this confidence are excluded.

limit.description: Maximum number of issues to display. Default: 100.

tools.name: TestReport
tools.title: Test Report
tools.description: Runs Wolfram Language test files (.wlt) and returns a report of the results

paths.description: Comma separated list of paths to Wolfram Language test files (.wlt) or directories of test files

timeConstraint.description: An optional time constraint (in seconds) for each test file

memoryConstraint.description: An optional memory constraint (in bytes) for each test file

newKernel.description: Whether to use a fresh kernel for running tests (default is true)

<result url='https://reference.wolfram.com/language/ref/ElectricCurrentPDEComponent#331170722'>

# ElectricCurrentPDEComponent > Examples > Applications > 3D Stationary Analysis > 2

Model a tungsten wire with a potential difference of 0.2 [Quantity[1, "Volts"]]. Set up the stationary current PDE model variables ``vars`` and ``pars`` :

```wl
In[1]:=
vars = {V[x, y, z], {x, y, z}};
pars = <|"Material" -> \[FreeformPrompt]["tungsten"]|>;
```

Set up the stationary current PDE:

```wl
In[2]:= op = ElectricCurrentPDEComponent[vars, pars];
```

The radius of the tungsten wire is 2.5·10^-3 [Quantity[1, "Meters"]] and the geometric shape of the wire is s-shaped. Specify the parameters of the geometry:

```wl
In[3]:=
L = 0.05;
r = 0.0025;
R = 0.0075;
```

The simulation domain:

```wl
In[4]:= Ω = <image removed>;
```

An electric potential boundary condition of Subscript[V, 0] = 0.2 [Quantity[1, "Volts"]] is applied at the left end boundary and a zero electric potential condition is applied at the right end boundary. A tolerance 0f 0.01 r is applied at both ends to account for numerical errors in the discretized domain.

Set the electric potential boundary conditions at both ends of the wire:

```wl
In[5]:= Subscript[Γ, potential] = {ElectricPotentialCondition[Abs[x] ≤ 0.01r && y^2 + z^2 ≤ r^2, vars, pars, <|"ElectricPotential" -> 0.2|>], ElectricPotentialCondition[Abs[y + r] ≤ 0.01r && (x - (L + 2R + r))^2 + z^2 ≤ r^2, vars, pars]};
```

Solve the PDE:

```wl
In[6]:= Vfun = NDSolveValue[{op == 0, Subscript[Γ, potential]}, V, {x, y, z}∈Ω]

Out[6]= InterpolatingFunction[{{0., 0.07}, {-0.0025, 0.0324991}, {-0.0025, 0.0025}}, <>]
```

Compute the current density vector:

```wl
In[7]:= Jfield = -QuantityMagnitude[pars["Material"]["ElectricalConductivity"]] * Grad[Vfun[x, y, z], {x, y, z}];
```

Visualize the current density magnitude:

```wl
In[8]:= SliceDensityPlot3D[Sqrt[Total[Jfield ^ 2]], {{"XStackedPlanes", 10}, {"YStackedPlanes", 12}, {"ZStackedPlanes", 3}}, {x, y, z}∈Ω, ...]

Out[8]= <image removed>
```

</result>

<result url='https://reference.wolfram.com/language/ref/SystemModelCalibrate#1874611642'>

# SystemModelCalibrate > Examples > Applications > Model Simplification

Recreate the behavior of a speaker by calibrating a simpler circuit using simulation results as input data:

```wl
In[1]:= speaker = <image removed>;

In[2]:= rl = <image removed>;
```

Compare the behavior of both models before calibration:

```wl
In[3]:= sims = SystemModelSimulate[speaker];

In[4]:= simrl = SystemModelSimulate[rl];

In[5]:= SystemModelPlot[{sims, simrl}, {"vs.v"}]

Out[5]= <image removed>
```

Retrieve simulation results as data and use them for calibration:

```wl
In[6]:= datav = sims["RawData", "vs.v"];

In[7]:= csmodel = SystemModelCalibrate[<|"vs.v" -> datav|>, {rl, 0.001 < l < 0.5}, {l}, "CalibratedSystemModel"]

Out[7]=
CalibratedSystemModel[Association["WLModel" -> False, "WLSamplingPeriod" -> Missing[], 
  "InputModelNameOrHead" -> "DocumentationExamples.Modeling.ElectricCircuit.SeriesRL", 
  "InputModel" -> Hold["DocumentationExamples.Modeling.ElectricCircuit.S ... 
   Hold[{Association["Name" -> "vs.v", "Data" -> CompressedData["«33117»"], "Unit" -> "V", 
      "AbsoluteValue" -> False, "DataType" -> "ListOfPairs", "DataStart" -> 0., "DataStop" -> 0.1, 
      "Weight" -> 1]}], "ValidationData" -> Hold[{}]]]
```

Compare the calibrated model with the speaker:

```wl
In[8]:= SystemModelPlot[{sims, csmodel["CalibratedSimulationData"]}, {"vs.v"}]

Out[8]= <image removed>
```

# Joule Heating of Tungsten Wire > Domain

The radius of the tungsten wire is r = 2.5·10^-3 [m]. The simulation domain Ω and the geometric shape of the wire are described in the following plot.

<image removed>

Specify the parameters of the geometry:

```wl
In[5]:=
L = 0.1;
r = 0.0025;
R = 0.0075;
```

Next, the 3D domain Ω is constructed by specifying the path of the tungsten wire.

Specify and visualize the centerline of the wire:

```wl
In[6]:=
arc1 = Table[R * {Cos[θ], Sin[θ], 0.}, {θ, -π / 2, π / 2, π / 30}];
arc2 = Reverse[-arc1];
arc3 = Table[R * {Cos[θ], Sin[θ], 0.}, {θ, π / 2, 0, -π / 30}];
pathPts = Join[...];

In[7]:= Graphics3D[{Thick, Blue, Line[pathPts]}, ...]

Out[7]= <image removed>
```

Construct the 3D tungsten wire:

```wl
In[8]:= wire = Graphics3D[{CapForm["Butt"], Tube[pathPts, r]}]

Out[8]= <image removed>
```

Now the boundary mesh region and the full element mesh can be generated. In order to get a good result, a grid finer than the default is used for the mesh generation.

Discretize the simulation domain:

```wl
In[9]:=
bmeshRegion = DiscretizeGraphics[wire];
mesh = ToElementMesh[bmeshRegion, MaxCellMeasure -> 5 * 10 ^ -10]

Out[9]= ElementMesh[{{0., 0.119986}, {-0.0025, 0.0324855}, {-0.00244537, 0.0025}}, {TetrahedronElement[<37525>]}]
```

In the following sections, the boundary conditions will be set up and the heat flux calculated at both ends and the side surfaces. To do so, the functions leftEndQ and rightEndQ are defined to determine whether a point {x, y, z} is located on the corresponding surface.

Set up the functions leftEndQ and rightEndQ to represent the wire's endpoint locations:

```wl
In[10]:=
tolerance = 0.01r;
leftEndQ[x_, y_, z_] := Abs[x] ≤ tolerance && y^2 + z^2 ≤ r^2
rightEndQ[x_, y_, z_] := Abs[y + r] ≤ tolerance && (x - (L + 2R + r))^2 + z^2 ≤ r^2
```

A tolerance of 0.01r is applied at both ends to account for numerical error in the discretized domain.

</result>

# Zumo path following robot > Sensor calibration

To carry out the calibration you will need a straight segment of the track and a protractor.

And we will use a [sketch](https://github.com/pololu/zumo-shield/blob/master/ZumoReflectanceSensorArray/examples/SensorCalibration/SensorCalibration.ino) already created by Pololu. The sketch is in the ZumoReflectanceSensorArray library that was installed earlier.

```wl
In[27]:= sensorCalibFile = FileNameJoin[{sketchBookDir, "ZumoReflectanceSensorArray", "examples", "SensorCalibration", "SensorCalibration.ino"}];

In[28]:= FileExistsQ[sensorCalibFile]

Out[28]= True
```

Open the sketch and the serial monior from the Arduino IDE, and upload the sketch.

<image removed>

```wl
In[29]:= (*RunProcess[$SystemShell,All,"open "<>sensorCalibFile] *)(* non-Mac?*)
```

After the sketch is uploaded the LED on the robot will turn on, and will remain on for about 10 seconds. In this period you should gently slide the robot back and forth across the track a couple of times so that the sensor is exposed to both the track and the background.

Following this , orient the robot at various angles relative to the track. Record the sensor readings and the corresponding angles.

```wl
In[30]:= sensorData = IconizedObject[«sensor data»];
```

Use LinearModeFit to model the relationship between the sensor readings and the orientation of the robot.

```wl
In[31]:= sensorFit = LinearModelFit[sensorData, r, r]

Out[31]= FittedModel[-0.523401 + 0.000228434 r]
```

Compare the actual and fitted values.

```wl
In[32]:= Show[ListLinePlot[Sort[sensorData], PlotStyle -> Dashed, FrameLabel -> {"Reading", "Angle (rad)"}], Plot[sensorFit[r], {r, 0, 5000}], Frame -> True, ImageSize -> Medium]

Out[32]= <image removed>
```

Create an input-output model to get the orientation from the sensor readings.

```wl
In[33]:= \[ScriptR]\[ScriptS] = NonlinearStateSpaceModel[{{}, sensorFit[r]}, {}, r, SamplingPeriod -> 0.001]

Out[33]= NonlinearStateSpaceModel[{{}, {-0.523401 + 0.000228434 r}}, {}, {r}, {Automatic}, Automatic, SamplingPeriod -> 0.001]
```

</result>

# GeometricOptimization > Examples > Applications > Circuit Problems > 2

Find the widths of n wire segments in an interconnected network in a circuit with known capacitance. There are five wire segments in the network below:

<image removed>

For each wire segment, the resistance Subscript[R, i] = α (l / Subscript[w, i]) and capacitances Subscript[S, i] = β l Subscript[w, i] + γ l, where α, β, γ, are positive constants depending on the wire properties and l is the length of the wire and width Subscript[w, i] :

```wl
In[1]:=
wireResistance = Table[Subscript[R, i] -> α(l / Indexed[w, i]), {i, 5}];
wireCapacitance = Table[Subscript[S, i] -> β * l * Indexed[w, i] + γ * l, {i, 5}];
```

Using a π model, each wire is modeled using a resistor and capacitor. The resulting network becomes a resistor-capacitor network:

<image removed>

The new capacitances of the model are obtained by summing the respective network capacitances with the wire capacitances Subscript[S, i] :

```wl
In[2]:=
rcCapacitance = {Subscript[Overscript[c, ~], 0] -> Subscript[S, 1], Subscript[Overscript[c, ~], 1] -> Subscript[c, 1] + Subscript[S, 1] + Subscript[S, 2] + Subscript[S, 4], Subscript[Overscript[c, ~], 2] -> Subscript[c, 2] + Subscript[S, 2] + Subscript[S, 4], 
	Subscript[Overscript[c, ~], 3] -> Subscript[c, 3] + Subscript[S, 3], Subscript[Overscript[c, ~], 4] -> Subscript[c, 4] + Subscript[S, 4] + Subscript[S, 5], Subscript[Overscript[c, ~], 5] -> Subscript[c, 5] + Subscript[S, 5]} /. wireCapacitance;
```

The Elmore delay measures the delay of voltage changing and converging to a new value. The Elmore delay for each capacitor k is Subscript[D, k] = Underoverscript[∑, i = 1, n]Subscript[Overscript[C, ~], i]Subscript[∑,  k∈V(i, k)]Subscript[R, k], where V(i, k) is the set of resistances between capacitors k and i :

```wl
In[3]:=
V = {...};
elmoreDelay = V.{Subscript[Overscript[c, ~], 0], Subscript[Overscript[c, ~], 1], Subscript[Overscript[c, ~], 2], Subscript[Overscript[c, ~], 3], Subscript[Overscript[c, ~], 4], Subscript[Overscript[c, ~], 5]} ;
```

The objective is to minimize the largest Elmore delay:

```wl
In[4]:= objective = Max@@elmoreDelay /. Join[wireResistance, rcCapacitance];
```

The wire is constrained to be within a range:

```wl
In[5]:= wireConstraint = 1\[VectorLessEqual]w\[VectorLessEqual]5;
```

The total area cannot exceed a maximum allowable area:

```wl
In[6]:= areaConstraint = l * Total[w] ≤ Subscript[A, max];
```

Specify the parameters:

```wl
In[7]:= params = {Subscript[R, 0] -> 0.1, l -> 1, α -> 1, β -> 1, γ -> 1, Subscript[A, max] -> 20, Subscript[c, 1] -> 10, Subscript[c, 2] -> 10, Subscript[c, 3] -> 10, Subscript[c, 4] -> 10, Subscript[c, 5] -> 10};
```

Find the width of the wires:

```wl
In[8]:=
GeometricOptimization[objective /. params, {wireConstraint, 
	areaConstraint} /. params, w∈Vectors[5]]

Out[8]= {w -> {5., 4.27962, 3.21087, 4.31292, 2.80182}}
```

</result>
